claims.text: Adding 2–3 vol% ductile Fe-rich nanoparticles during rapid solidification, followed by annealing at 600–700 °C, will improve the mechanical performance of MnNiSi-based alloys.
The proposed treatment will retain the sharp magnetocaloric transition of the baseline MnNiSi-based alloy.
The baseline melt-processed MnNiSi-based alloy has a homogeneous microstructure.
The baseline MnNiSi-based alloy has a well-defined magnetocaloric effect.
Annealing at 600–700 °C will promote uniform dispersion of the Fe-rich nanoparticles.
Annealing at 600–700 °C can disperse the nanoparticles without significant interdiffusion.
Rapid solidification minimizes phase segregation in the proposed MnNiSi-based composite.
Annealing under an inert atmosphere at 600–700 °C will preserve the MnNiSi matrix composition and prevent excessive Fe diffusion.
Excessive Fe diffusion could disrupt magnetic ordering in the MnNiSi matrix.
Keeping the Fe-rich nanoparticle fraction below approximately 3 vol% limits perturbation of magnetic exchange interactions.
The treatment will produce a uniformly dispersed Fe-rich second phase within the MnNiSi matrix.
Dispersed ductile Fe-rich nanoparticles will blunt crack tips and arrest or impede crack propagation.
The Fe-rich nanoparticles will redistribute local stresses during mechanical loading.
The Fe-rich nanoparticles will hinder dislocation movement.
The low nanoparticle volume fraction will minimize alteration of magnetic exchange pathways and thereby maintain the magnetocaloric transition.
Relative to the baseline, the modified alloy will have greater fracture toughness.
Relative to the baseline, the modified alloy will have greater fatigue resistance.
The modified alloy's magnetic entropy-change magnitude and transition sharpness will remain comparable to those of the baseline.
Conventionally melt-processed MnNiSi-based alloys exhibit standard mechanical brittleness and a large magnetocaloric effect.
Exceeding the proposed nanoparticle fraction or annealing window may degrade magnetocaloric properties or cause phase changes.

contradictions.description: The stated baseline is produced by standard or conventional melt processing, whereas the experiment says all samples, including the 0% baseline, are processed by rapid solidification and annealing. Thus the experimental control does not match the stated baseline.
